## Completed assessment and principal findings

This assessment was carried out on 7 October 2026 against the locally
available LISS releases and lissr source commit
`76aaa6a6547b89d1fc8be5b730be94087e2eb60e` (development version
1.4.1.9000). It examined all ten core modules and the monthly Background
Variables collection. It is a diagnosis of observed problems and a roadmap,
not a new cleaner. The [Income Cleaning](income-cleaning.html) framework
continues to target household income; none of the additional interventions
described here has been implemented as part of this assessment.

The largest confirmed coding exposures were undeclared nonresponse in
Income 2023 and Assets 2020. A diagnostic execution showed that the Income
codes can reach the existing household-income cleaner as numerical values.
Response-format changes and loss of a substantive outsourcing category
create additional comparability problems. Health activity and Culture and
Sports time entries contain impossible durations; the 2025 inflation
probability battery has frequent internal contradictions. Health
measurements and life-event chronologies contain smaller but analytically
important groups of implausible or contradictory values.
The evidence does **not** support describing every module as badly corrupted:
respondent keys were complete and unique within every selected file, and
several screened batteries showed no domain violations.

### Scope, sources and counting

The collection contained 169 core SAV files. The higher available release,
`cd10c_EN_1.1p.sav`, was selected instead of `cd10c_EN_1.0p.sav`, giving
168 selected core releases. All 221 monthly Background Variables SAV
snapshots were included. The duplicate Housing release was compared
separately and had identical values on all shared columns; the higher
release omits one free-text dwelling-location column. A separate
`WorkSchoolingW10_isco08.sav` occupation supplement was checked without
counting it as another survey wave. The inventory therefore comprised
391 SAV files and 173 PDF references, with 389 selected survey snapshots.
ZIP, DTA and CSV copies were not counted as
additional observations. These choices define this assessment's corpus;
they are not a proposed automatic release-selection policy for lissr.

| Collection | Selected files | Observed rows | Available span |
|:--|--:|--:|:--|
| Assets (CA) | 10 | 55,849 | ca08a–ca25j |
| Housing (CD) | 18 | 66,207 | cd08a–cd25r |
| Family and Household (CF) | 17 | 100,219 | cf08a–cf24q |
| Health (CH) | 18 | 101,691 | ch07a–ch25r |
| Economic Integration: Income (CI) | 18 | 97,557 | ci08a–ci25r |
| Personality (CP) | 18 | 101,651 | cp08a–cp26r |
| Religion and Ethnicity (CR) | 18 | 105,792 | cr08a–cr25r |
| Culture and Sports (CS) | 18 | 105,309 | cs08a–cs25r |
| Politics and Values (CV) | 18 | 108,013 | cv08a–cv26r |
| Work and Schooling (CW) | 15 | 85,270 | cw11d–cw25r |
| Background Variables | 221 | 2,436,395 | November 2007–March 2026 |

There were 927,558 core respondent-wave rows and 2,436,395 background
person-month rows, not that many different participants. The background
collection contained 34,304 distinct respondents. The inventory recorded
48,792 file-column instances, of which 46,817 were numeric. All selected
files were read; metadata and respondent keys were checked throughout, and
the semantic constraints reported below were applied to their relevant
fields across the available waves. This was not an exhaustive validation of
every possible cross-variable relationship or of every free-text response.

The investigation combined observed distributions, SPSS labels and
user-missing declarations, questionnaire bounds, routing and units,
within-row logical constraints, and selected longitudinal checks. It also
compared the findings with the current recipes and household-income rules.
The initial assessment was extended by two separately frozen external
assessments and independently checked against the raw SAVs with R/haven,
the relevant questionnaires, and selected executions of existing package
functions. Agreement between reports was not used as validation. The
counts below incorporate corrected field inventories and eligibility
definitions; source identities and aggregate verification records were
retained privately. No respondent-level data are included in this article.
Intentional nonresponse, structural absence, instrument redesigns and
already handled sentinel regimes were not counted as new respondent errors.
Endpoint labels were interpreted as scale endpoints, not as the only legal
responses. Category-coded years were decoded before temporal comparisons.

Counts are unweighted descriptions of these releases. Each denominator is
the eligible set for that particular check, after the stated missing-code
handling. A cell, a complete response set, a respondent-wave and an adjacent
monthly transition are different counting units. Overlapping checks are not
summed into an overall error rate. A screening flag estimates the workload
for review; it is not automatically a confirmed erroneous observation.

### How the priorities were determined

The order below combines six considerations: observed prevalence, severity
of the inconsistency, strength of detection, confidence in correction,
downstream analytical impact, and risk of changing a legitimate response.
The ordering is a documented judgment, not a fitted score. High-prevalence
encoding failures with defensible invalid-to-missing treatment come first;
plausible but unverified remappings require confirmation. Frequent logical
contradictions follow, even when only flagging is defensible. Rare open-ended
extremes with no reliable replacement rank last.

| Priority | Problem group | Main observed evidence | Defensible disposition |
|--:|:--|:--|:--|
| 1 | [Nonresponse codes surviving as amounts or categories](#source-specific-nonresponse-encoding-a-prerequisite-for-numerical-cleaning) | CI23p: 2,293/4,353 household amounts; CA20g: 5,857 cells in 2,849/5,849 rows; CH: 4,992 labelled undeclared cells | Source-scoped classification; typed missing amounts or explicit unknown categories, retaining raw codes |
| 2 | [Coding, response-format and category-preservation gaps](#coding-and-construct-comparability-scale-changes-and-lost-categories) | CV: 17,391 exposed ratings; CS12e: 17,524 no answers at a different code; CF: 1,697 outsourcing cells swept | Verified semantic crosswalks or separate representations; abstain on unresolved mappings |
| 3 | [CH and CS time-entry failures](#health-and-culture-and-sports-time-entry-failures-with-disproportionate-impact) | CH: 2,355/165,334 daily-hour entries above 24; CS: 142/811,036 daily pairs above 24 hours | Strong domain flags; invalid-to-missing where justified, no assumed unit repair |
| 4 | [Probability and ordered-expectation inconsistencies](#probabilities-and-expectation-intervals-internally-inconsistent-sets) | CI25r: 1,403/4,511 complete probability grids (31.10%) | Flag/review; no unique automatic numerical repair |
| 5 | [CH height and weight](#health-implausible-anthropometry-and-unstable-derived-bmi) | 176/101,574 height flags; 142/101,480 weight flags | Conservative plausibility flags; tightly supported unit candidates only |
| 6 | [Clinical use, durations and life-event chronology](#clinical-use-durations-and-life-event-chronology-inconsistent-combinations) | Conflicting service-use answers and impossible age/event combinations in CH, CW and CF | Flag; auxiliary recovery only with validated independent evidence |
| 7 | [Background demographic and roster disagreements](#background-variables-demographic-and-roster-disagreements) | Partner/roster boundary: 7,340/352,566 person-months; 11/2,436,395 roster-size disagreements; 102 adjacent-month birth-year changes | Review, respecting top-coding, snapshot completeness and uncertain source precedence |
| 8 | [Income-period candidates and other monetary, housing and workload tails](#income-period-candidates-and-other-financial-housing-and-workload-tails) | Annual-income screens reveal small amounts; open tails and component conflicts remain ambiguous | Review with reference-period evidence; no automatic multiplication or clipping |

Follow a problem-group link for its measured diagnosis and correction
limits. The [ordered to-do list](#ordered-to-do-list-derived-from-the-assessment)
uses the same priorities and specifies the safeguards and expected benefit.

## Diagnosed problem areas

### 1. Source-specific nonresponse encoding: a prerequisite for numerical cleaning

#### Income 2023: undeclared codes reach the existing cleaner

`ci23p_EN_1.0p.sav` contains negative ten-digit codes that neither its
seven-digit value labels nor its missing declarations describe correctly:

| Field | Raw finite answers | `-9999999999` | `-9999999998` | Combined coded fraction |
|:--|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| ci23p337, annual taxable income | 4,828 | 1,998 | 682 | 55.51% |
| ci23p338, estimated annual taxable income follow-up | 1,416 | 934 | 455 | 98.09% |
| ci23p339, household net income | 4,353 | 2,293 | 0 | 52.68% |

The questionnaire specifies bounded euro amounts and nonresponse options,
not these enormous losses. For household income, 2,292 of the 2,293 coded
answers have the follow-up that is routed only after "don't know". That
provides strong same-wave evidence for this subtype. The taxable-income
follow-up does not distinguish the two options sufficiently to assign
their subtypes with the same confidence. Adjacent-wave labels alone cannot
resolve the conflicting label order in this release.

A complete execution of the existing CI merge retained all 2,293 household
codes in `s339` and returned `valid_for_analysis = TRUE`. A subsequent
diagnostic cleaner run, explicitly binding `variables = list(target =
"s339")`, with otherwise default settings and no background frame, found
none through residual-missing rule P06 and sign-rectified all through P03.
In `mode = "flag"`, it proposed finite replacements for 1,282 and missing
values for 1,011; all original values remained unchanged. This is a
measured unsafe proposal path, not a claim that those proposals were
applied. A default cleaner call on that merge instead stops because its
default aliases do not include `s339`; supplied target names and panel
context matter. Source-code inspection alone would not establish these
configuration-specific outcomes.

The immediate need is a source-aware nonresponse check before sign
rectification, donor selection or scale correction. Numerical imputation
does not resolve an encoding defect. The existing household-income
framework is therefore not evidence that all CI missing regimes are
already safe.

#### Assets 2020: two undocumented code families

`ca20g_EN_1.0p.sav` has **5,857 undocumented nonresponse cells in 27
fields**, affecting **2,849/5,849 respondents (48.71%)**. These comprise:

* 3,072 amount cells at `-9999999999` or `-9999999998` in suffixes
  `012`, `016`, `035`, `083`, `085`, affecting 2,638 respondents. The
  banking-balance field `012` contains 2,513 of them.
* 2,785 cells at `-9` or `-8` in 22 other amount, bracket and yes/no fields,
  affecting 1,624 respondents. The field list is `013`–`028`, `036`,
  `055`, `056`, `063`, `064`, `084`, `086`, excluding `016` from that
  interval. The two respondent sets overlap and must not be added.

The source specifies signed amount bounds for `012`, `016`, `083`, `085`,
positive bounds for other amounts, and nonnegative response categories.
Its documented nonresponse forms differ from the observed codes. Small
`-9`/`-8` values do not occur on the five large-code fields in this release;
they are restricted to the other 22 fields. All 5,857 codes fall outside
the relevant documented amount/category domains. This is a release-level
encoding failure, not evidence that half the respondents supplied wrong
substantive wealth values.

Amount-to-bracket routing supports the nonresponse interpretation:
2,375/2,378 amount cells in the apparent don't-know family have the bracket
follow-up, versus none of 2,520 in the apparent refusal family. These
denominators cover amount codes, not every bracket or binary code. Exact
DK/refusal assignments on the remaining fields remain inferential.
Later-wave metadata provide supporting comparisons but are not uniform
across every amount and bracket field.

Current rule `B03_ca20g_largeneg_review` adds a review flag to **all 5,849
rows of the wave**, rather than detecting just the code-bearing cells.
It does not remove either code family. Consequently the existing flag is
useful awareness of the release problem, but is not a value-level safeguard
for wealth calculations.

#### Health: labelled unknown answers without missing declarations

An independently verified subset contains 1,358 zero-euro "don't know"
cells: 813 in `ch13g249` and 250/122/173 in `ch13g264`, `ch15h264`,
`ch16i264`. Both labels and the same-wave questionnaires establish the
meaning, but zero is undeclared missing and the current CH recipe has no
corresponding recode. An execution of the existing user-missing sweep
retained all 1,358; a declared-zero control in `ch17j264` was removed.
This count is the labelled subset, not a census of every questionnaire-only
unknown code. Zero in an unrelated amount field may be a genuine amount.

Including categorical unknown answers gives **4,992 labelled undeclared
cells** under the following explicit source contracts:

| Source scope | Code meaning | Cells |
|:--|:--|--:|
| ch08b–ch13g, suffix 124 | 3, don't know expected health-problem duration | 1,472 |
| The four amount fields above | 0, don't know premium/allowance amount | 1,358 |
| ch13g263 | 5, don't know allowance application status | 484 |
| ch19l260 and ch20m260 | 99, don't know voluntary deductible | 1,453 |
| ch24q272 and ch25r272 | 4, don't know menopause status | 225 |

Labels and questionnaire categories identify these as nonresponse, but
the existing source-declaration sweep retained all 4,992 in an isolated
execution. That probe tests the sweep, not a complete CH merge. Many later
occurrences of the same numeric codes are already declared missing and
handled; a global code-3/4/5/99 recode would damage substantive categories.
Preserve unknown as a typed reason alongside the source response, with an
explicit analysis policy rather than treating it as a quantity or scale point.
The 3,634 categorical DK choices are legitimate responses if analysed as
explicit unknown categories; they are not 3,634 respondent errors requiring
deletion. The 1,358 amount codes must not be interpreted as known zero euros.

**Detection and correction limits.** Match exact codes only under a
verified release, field, label/routing and unit contract. Conversion of
confirmed nonresponse to missing is high-confidence normalization; preserve
the raw code and its reason separately. Retain an unknown subtype where
the evidence cannot distinguish DK from refusal. An invalid-to-missing
policy is preferable to inventing an amount. Never infer that every negative
balance or every zero is missing: ordinary negative equity occurs in
`ca20g035` despite its printed positive bound and requires separate source
review, not a blanket sign sweep.

**Priority rationale.** CI23p and CA20g have very large within-wave
exposures, direct effects on income/wealth estimates, and exact code-level
detection. CI23p additionally exposes a tested path into the current
cleaner's numerical proposals. Typed missing normalization is more
defensible and less risky than reconstructing an intended amount. These
checks must precede broader numerical-cleaning extensions.

### 2. Coding and construct comparability: scale changes and lost categories

#### Politics and Values: a systematic party-rating scale discrepancy

Four fields have no observed zero and occupy the range 1–11, although both
the questionnaire and their endpoint labels specify a 0–10 sympathy scale:

| Source file | Field | Nonmissing substantive ratings | Ratings equal to 11 |
|:--|:--|--:|--:|
| cv17i_EN_1.0p.sav | cv17i264 (DENK) | 4,249 | 10 |
| cv17i_EN_1.0p.sav | cv17i265 (VNL) | 3,653 | 8 |
| cv18j_EN_1.0p.sav | cv18j264 (DENK) | 4,961 | 22 |
| cv18j_EN_1.0p.sav | cv18j305 (Forum voor Democratie) | 4,528 | 47 |

The 87 values equal to 11 are definite violations of the published scale.
All 17,391 substantive ratings are exposed to a possible one-point offset;
they are **not** 17,391 individually proven mistakes. The published codebook
summary tables also report 1–11 for these fields. Other party ratings in
the same files, and these party series in subsequent waves, use 0–10.
The current CV recipe does not resolve this particular discrepancy.

**Detection and correction limits.** A release-and-field whitelist, the
questionnaire endpoints, the complete observed support and the published
summary tables make detection strong. Subtracting one from every
substantive value is a plausible coding repair and would restore the full
scale, but the direction of the coding error still needs confirmation from
the archive or original questionnaire export. Until that mapping is
confirmed, flag the affected fields and prevent unqualified pooling.
Neither clipping 11 to 10 nor shifting only the 87 visible violations
repairs a possible whole-field offset. The `999` nonresponse code must
retain its own meaning and must not enter an arithmetic remapping.

#### Culture and Sports: loneliness and holiday categories change meaning

CS loneliness suffixes `284`–`289` use `1 = yes`, `2 = no`, `3 = don't
know/don't want to say` in `cs12e`, whereas the other 17 available waves use
`1 = yes`, `2 = more or less`, `3 = no`. The questionnaire confirms this
response-format break. CS12e contains 35,742 cells from 5,957 respondents:
16,535 yes, 17,524 no and 1,683 nonresponse. The generic missing sweep
already removes the 1,683 declared code-3 cells; that part is not an
unhandled missing-code leak. The unresolved problem is that naive pooling
would interpret the 17,524 no answers as the other waves' middle category.

A semantic representation of no is identifiable, but the missing middle
response cannot be recovered and a crosswalk does not establish measurement
equivalence. Preserve an instrument-period flag; qualified binary scoring
or a measurement model requires an explicit analytical decision. Do not
map source code 2 to 3 in place while leaving the original "3 is missing"
declaration active, because the later sweep could then delete the newly
mapped substantive no answers. A separately derived representation with
appropriate metadata is safer.

Holiday counts `102`/`103` use `1 = not once` through `6 = five times or
more` before `cs23p`, then `0 = not once` through `5 = five times or more`
in `cs23p`–`cs25r`. Both questionnaire versions confirm the change. The
last three waves contain 16,056 domestic and 16,055 abroad responses,
involving 6,815 people. These responses are correctly coded within their
wave, but the current recipe has no semantic crosswalk. A release-specific
category mapping can remove an artificial one-code change exactly; retain
the top category as **five or more**, not an exact count of five.

#### Family and Household: outsourcing is lost from merged categorical fields

In CF task-division items `483`–`488`, code 9 means that all work is
outsourced. It is observed in 1,948 cells across `cf15h`–`cf24q`, affecting
1,525 respondent-waves and 870 people. The first wave retains it, whereas
the other nine declare it user-missing. A full execution of the current
CF merge converted exactly 1,697 cells in those nine waves to NA and
retained the 251 in `cf15h`, while reporting `valid_for_analysis = TRUE`.
The existing sweep log discloses affected-cell counts; source answers and
files remain intact. The problem is inconsistent preservation of a real
category in the merged representation.

Code 9 is outside the ordered 1–5 division-of-work scale. Treating complete
outsourcing as not applicable to that ordinal score is defensible; the
source declaration alone does not prove a publisher mistake. A future
solution should preserve the categorical response and an outsourcing
indicator, with a separately named 1–5 score using typed not-applicable
missingness. Simply vetoing the sweep would allow 9 into numerical means
and ordinal models. Exported missing metadata must also preserve the
categorical representation consistently.

#### Income labels and education taxonomy: preserve semantics before arithmetic

`ci15h005` has 5,893 correctly stored 0–10 ladder ratings, including six
zeros, but its value labels describe a shifted 1–11 coding. The same-wave
questionnaire and published statistics confirm the data's 0–10 scale.
Current A-02 is `note_only`: executing it changes no values, and its
documentary `transform_ref` is not applied as arithmetic. A future
subtract-one action based on that premise would damage all ratings and
create six negatives. The needed repair is verified metadata alignment,
not numerical rescaling. Conversely, some CI22o nonresponse labels reverse
the questionnaire's DK/refusal meanings; preserve uncertainty rather than
guessing from the label alone.

CW highest education attended (`008`, merged `s008`, recipe alias `q008`) has genuine taxonomy
changes. Of 32,467 answers after the 2020 redesign, 447 use changed primary
education codes; 1,608 answers in `cw24q`/`cw25r` use revised MBO categories.
The older BOL/BBL tracks and newer MBO qualification levels are different
dimensions, so no one-to-one replacement is justified. These are exposure
counts, not erroneous respondents. A documented coarser taxonomy may permit
some comparisons, with explicit lost-detail and unmapped-category flags.
The existing education rule does work for recipe target `q005` (merged
`s005`): all 80,055 observed values were mapped in a complete CW merge,
while the item is structurally absent in `cw19l`. The gap is education
attended, not a failed `q005` executor.

**Priority rationale.** These problems expose whole response blocks to
wrong meanings or inconsistent category loss. Verified holiday crosswalks,
label alignment and category-preserving representations are comparatively
low-risk; CV remapping and education/measurement equivalence require more
evidence. Their breadth and influence on longitudinal analyses place them
above isolated outliers, but source-specific uncertainty prevents a single
blanket correction rule.

### 3. Health and Culture and Sports: time-entry failures with disproportionate impact

#### Health activity: impossible daily hours and ambiguous unit representations

Across `ch07a`–`ch18k`, activity/sitting hour fields `186`, `189`, `192`,
`194` contain 2,355/165,334 observed entries above 24 hours per day
(1.42%), affecting 2,200 respondent-waves and 1,806 people. Of those
entries, 1,903 lie between 25 and 60; 2,020 have empty or zero minute
companions. These patterns suggest minutes entered into an hour field,
but they do not uniquely establish that explanation or an intended number.
The activity items were **deleted** from `ch19l`; later-wave duration
bounds do not retrospectively constrain them.

The CH minute companions are unbounded integer/empty inputs and may express
a whole duration rather than a residual component. They do not have the
source-bounded CS 0–59 contract. Therefore a minute value above 59 is not
automatically invalid. Exact hour/minute patterns need separate review
against the question's representation. In 5,256/84,323 complete pairs
(6.23%, involving 2,190 people), positive hours and minutes satisfy
`minutes = 60 * hours`. This is a repeated-entry pattern, not a count of
confirmed duplicate-duration errors. Equality can reflect two expressions
of the same duration, but is not proof that
an additive answer should be halved. Empty minutes are not known zero.
Daily hours above 24 are a strong source-unit contradiction; division by
60, conversion from a supposed weekly period or deletion of a duplicate
component would require independent evidence.

#### Culture and Sports: bounded components and propagated totals

The complete CS hour-and-minute inventory found 142/811,036 evaluable daily pairs
(0.018%) above 24 hours. Two minute components exceed the explicitly
specified 0–59 range: `cs15h200` and `cs16i232`. Six nonmissing smartphone
weekly-hour values exceed 168 hours, and `cs16i125` contains one TV-hours
entry beyond its specified range. The union of daily/weekly time-budget
failures affects 96/104,772 evaluable respondent-wave rows (0.092%).
The pair and row counts differ because several time fields can fail in
the same response.

All 811,036 complete hour/minute/derived-total triples checked in the
collection satisfy `total_minutes = 60 * hours + minutes`. The calculated
helpers therefore reproduce the bad inputs faithfully; they are not
independent confirmation of the reported duration. In `cs15h387`, excluding
the observation with the invalid minute input changes the raw mean from
6,041.72 to 69.10 minutes. This is a descriptive sensitivity calculation,
not a cleaned estimate or a justification for excluding other high values.

**Detection and correction limits.** Validate each question's daily or
weekly period, integer minute bounds and the corresponding single-activity
time budget. Minute bounds must come from the particular source; the CS
0–59 rule must not be transferred to CH. Activities may overlap, so summing
unrelated activities and
demanding a total below 24 hours is not defensible. Invalid components can
be flagged and, under an explicit policy, set to missing together with the
dependent derived total. A helper calculated from the same component
cannot recover its intended value. Do not convert a large entry to hours,
divide by ten, or carry excess minutes into hours without independent
source evidence.

**Priority rationale.** Impossible CH daily hours are appreciably more
frequent than the rare CS failures, while a CS error can change a mean
by orders of magnitude. Explicit units and the bounded CS structure make
safe detection and invalid-to-missing treatment practical. Numerical
reconstruction is much less certain.

### 4. Probabilities and expectation intervals: internally inconsistent sets

In `ci25r_EN_1.0p.sav`, 1,403 of 4,511 complete, in-domain inflation
probability grids (31.10%) violate at least one necessary probability
constraint. The four fields are `ci25r431`–`ci25r434`; `ci25r430` determines
their displayed inflation thresholds. All 4,511 conditioning codes were
valid. The first two probabilities concern being below increasing
thresholds, and the last two concern being above increasing thresholds.
Consequently, `431 <= 432` and `433 >= 434`; each of the four low-tail /
high-tail pairs concerns disjoint events and must sum to at most 100.
The count is the union of these checks, not their sum. Even allowing five
percentage points of tolerance, 1,117 grids (24.76%) fail.

Two additional ordered intervals fail in the same release: expected income
minimum `ci25r425` exceeds maximum `ci25r426` in 122/4,147 complete pairs
(2.94%), and expected inflation minimum `ci25r428` exceeds maximum
`ci25r429` in 216/4,514 pairs (4.79%). These counts can overlap with the
probability-grid failures. A six-level income-evaluation sequence in the
earlier CI collection (`230`–`235`) has 813/53,261 complete sets with an order inversion
(1.53%).

CH survival expectations (`006`–`010`, recorded on a 0–10 probability scale)
provide a second application: 1,063/90,259
evaluable respondent-wave sets (1.18%) contain an increase in the stated
probability of reaching a higher target age. Detection uses the nested
events represented by the age-specific questions, not a requirement that
optimism or health beliefs remain stable over time.

**Detection and correction limits.** Reconstruct the exact displayed
thresholds, routing and reference horizon for the particular wave; check
bounds, nested-event order, disjoint-event sums and minimum–maximum order.
A negative expected inflation rate is legitimate and is not a missing
code merely because it is negative. These checks establish internal
incoherence, not that a particular economic forecast or health belief is
wrong. Swapping interval endpoints, sorting probabilities or projecting
them onto a coherent distribution would impose an unverified error model.
Default to flagging the response set; any analysis that excludes it or
treats it as missing should preserve the original answers and report a
sensitivity analysis. Automated numerical replacement is not justified.

**Priority rationale.** CI25r has high block-level prevalence and strong
logical detection. The problems can distort estimates of expectations and
uncertainty, but the absence of a unique repair keeps this below source-specific
nonresponse normalization, comparability safeguards and bounded time
failures. Correctability is one criterion, not a reason to dismiss strong
joint constraints. The household-income cleaner does not validate these
belief batteries.

### 5. Health: implausible anthropometry and unstable derived BMI

Across the 18 CH releases, height suffix `016` has 176/101,574 nonmissing
values outside a deliberately broad screening interval of 100–230 cm
(0.17%); weight suffix `017` has 142/101,480 outside 20–300 kg (0.14%).
There are 26 heights below 50 cm and 96 weights below 10 kg. The union of
the height and weight screens is 314/101,574 respondent-wave rows (173
different people), with four rows flagged on both measures. The broad
intervals are review thresholds, not universal
biological limits or questionnaire bounds. No observed height or weight
violates the permissive instrument ranges of 1–300 cm and 1–1,000 kg.

Wrong units, misplaced decimals and incomplete entries are plausible
explanations for some of these values. BMI depends on squared height, so a
single scale error can dominate a derived health measure even when the
overall flagged fraction is small. Distributional extremes alone do not
prove which component is wrong. A conservative temporal screen found only
one height observation whose factor-of-ten candidate agreed within 2 cm
with both the preceding and following adult height records. Height answers
are already preloaded from the previous wave in `ch08b`, so repeated neighbouring values
are not automatically independent measurements. The candidate remains
unverified.

**Detection and correction limits.** Check units and questionnaire bounds
first, then examine broad plausibility, derived BMI and within-person
changes together. Keep hard instrument violations separate from soft
anthropometric flags. A factor-of-ten or unit-conversion candidate needs
independent agreement, compatible timing, a unique admissible candidate
and preserved competing explanations. Two neighbouring observations are
supporting evidence, not proof; illness, amputation, pregnancy and genuine
weight change preclude indiscriminate smoothing. Unresolved values should
remain flagged or be treated as missing under an explicit analytical
policy, with no automatic clipping to a population percentile.

**Priority rationale.** The observed prevalence is modest, but height errors
have disproportionate effects on BMI and health models. Detectability is
useful, while conservative correction is possible only for a small,
well-supported subset. That combination places this above general
open-ended monetary outlier handling.

### 6. Clinical use, durations and life-event chronology: inconsistent combinations

CH suffix `228` reports no specialist visit while suffix `208` records a
positive number of hospital-specialist visits in 1,123/96,851 evaluable
respondent-wave rows (1.16%). Both questions refer to the preceding twelve
months. The mismatch affects 1,003 people and is more common than a rare
single numerical typo. It can change estimated healthcare use, but the
answers do not identify which field is mistaken. Do not infer a zero count
from the binary response, or reverse the binary response from the count,
without independent evidence.
The eligible set includes four observed counts at 999: this is the allowed
upper endpoint and has no nonresponse label/declaration on these source
fields. Restricting counts to below 999 gives 1,120/96,847 instead, but
that is a different screen, not a failed reproduction of the larger set.

CH illness-duration components (`107`–`110`) exceed the respondent's age plus one year
in 83/8,961 evaluable sets (0.93%); nonworking-duration components do so in
33/5,040 (0.65%; nonworking fields `101`–`103`, plus `268` where present).
Their union is 109/9,295 evaluable respondent-wave rows.
The check compares each component separately, expressing
months, weeks or days in years, rather than assuming that early-wave
duration entries are additive. Before ch19l the components may be alternative
units for a total duration; modern residual-component limits must not be
applied retrospectively. Fourteen of 7,683 reported illness-year
components resemble a calendar year rather than an elapsed duration.
That resemblance is a flag, not evidence that subtracting it from the
interview year reconstructs the answer.

CW has 70 pre-birth employment-event field/wave inconsistencies in 85,886
eligible checks after decoding category-coded years: employer start (`134`)
24/45,232, stopping work 30/33,361, starting job search 12/6,446 and starting
a care-related work reduction (`454`) 4/847. The other event fields are
work stop `319` and job-search start `340`; respondent birth year is `002`.
Actual retirement age (`119` in early waves, `535` from 2015) exceeds current
age plus one in 9/1,987 eligible pairs. In CF, the conservative chronology
screens found 48/14,920 parent death-before-birth pairs, 78/106,913 biological
parent birth-year comparisons, 108/133,486 relationship-date comparisons
and 43/141,657 biological child-before-parent birth-year comparisons.
These denominators count eligible field/wave comparisons, not unique
people; the checks can overlap. Their calendar-year eligibility screen is
1800 through survey year plus one; other years need separate domain and
provenance review rather than being counted as additional ordering evidence.

The CF parent pairs are father `005`/`008` and mother `009`/`012`;
relationship dates are `028`, `029` and `031`. Child birth-year fields
are `037`–`051` through 2014 and `456`–`470` from 2015, qualified by
biological-parent status in `098`–`112`.

**Detection and correction limits.** Decode year categories using the
wave's labels, distinguish actual from planned retirement, and identify
biological versus step/adoptive relationships. Where respondent birth
year is inferred from preloaded age, use a conservative year interval
that allows birthday timing; do not compare against a falsely precise
point estimate. The CF screen used `survey_year - age - 1` through
`survey_year - age + 1`, with preloaded age `004`. Events trigger only below
the lower bound, and biological-parent birth years only at or above the
upper bound. Selected-child roster slots cannot be assumed to refer
to the same child over time. Nine of 9,958 valid selected-child/roster
comparisons disagree in the unambiguous 2015–2024 roster scheme (`001`
selects the slot; `002` is the derived birth year), offering a potential auxiliary-source repair only
after the index and roster are independently validated.

Impossible ordering identifies an inconsistent combination, not necessarily
the erroneous field. Correct a date or duration only when an independent,
correctly identified source uniquely resolves it. Otherwise flag the set
and preserve the original; arithmetic onset-year conversions, endpoint
swaps and interpolation would require unjustified assumptions.

**Priority rationale.** Conflicting service-use answers and chronology can affect employment histories,
retirement timing, family-event analyses and duration models. Strong
constraints reveal real inconsistencies, but prevalence is generally low
and error localization is difficult. This ranks below the more prevalent
or more directly bounded groups above.

### 7. Background Variables: demographic and roster disagreements

The monthly collection has no duplicate respondent-month keys and no
observed age-versus-birth-year discrepancy greater than one year. However,
102/2,401,631 eligible adjacent-month transitions change birth year;
50 decrease age and 35 increase it by more than one year. Birth-year
changes affect 102 people. These are discrepancies for review, not proof
that the later value is wrong: administrative corrections can improve a
previously mistaken record. Eighty-one monthly age records exceed a soft
120-year review threshold, representing four people rather than 81 separate
cases; age must not be capped automatically. Urbanization field `sted`
contains an unlabelled `-99` in 108 observations across 27 snapshots
(November 2022–January 2025), a possible missing-code omission whose
meaning also requires confirmation.

Across the whole monthly history, 131 people have more than one valid
birth year and 42 have a span above 20 years, excluding the placeholder
year 1. Ninety-two people have both recorded `geslacht` codes 1 and 2;
18 also have the large birth-year discontinuity. These patterns merit
identity/provenance review, but do not establish identifier reuse or which
record should be replaced. Changes in recorded sex/gender are not inherently
errors and must not be smoothed automatically.

After respecting the codebook's top-coding of `aantalhh` and `aantalki` at
9 (nine or more), while also accepting exact counts above 9 in older
releases, 11/2,436,395 person-month rows disagree between reported
household size and the observed household roster (four people, three
households). In 23 rows
(13 people), the child count is at least the household size while household
size is below 9. A roster disagreement alone does not establish a wrong
household-size value unless completeness of the monthly roster is known.
The comparison is household-and-month specific; changes in household
membership are expected.

A larger release-period discrepancy affects the partner indicator:
7,340/352,566 person-months in September 2014–May 2017 (361 people) have
`partner = 0` while the same household-month roster lists a partner position;
four additional rows occur in February 2008. In June 2017, all 100 members
listed as partners in the 100 affected May households remain in the same
household; 87 positions become unknown, six become child/housemate and seven
remain partner-coded. Many household heads are widowed, but widowhood does
not exclude a later unwedded partner. These observations confirm a
recording/reclassification boundary, not that the listed members were dead,
had departed, or that either source is certainly stale. A roster-derived
overwrite of `partner` or household size is therefore unsupported.

**Detection and correction limits.** Check respondent-month identity,
birth-year and age agreement with birthday tolerance, household membership,
top-coding and the codebook's definition of a child. A child living at home
is not necessarily younger than 14, which also matters for equivalised
income. Exact monthly linkage is already a separate lissr capability and
must not be replaced with nearest-month matching. Do not overwrite a
reported count with the observed roster count when the roster may be
incomplete, or choose a modal birth year without a source-precedence rule.
Preserve review flags and allow a verified administrative correction to
remain a genuine change in the recorded data.

**Priority rationale.** These fields are ubiquitous covariates and income
denominators, so discrepancies deserve an auditable check. The partner
boundary adds a larger review group, but uncertainty over source precedence
and the small fractions for the hard demographic checks put this
below the more severe groups. The findings do not support wholesale
demographic smoothing or reconstruction.

### 8. Income-period candidates and other financial, housing and workload tails

#### Small annual components: a period-confusion hypothesis, not a measured error rate

Several annual CI component fields contain many small positive amounts.
The same-wave questionnaires establish annual units, but the following
thresholds and candidate windows are analyst-chosen screens:

| Component and source suffix | Positive answers | Below screening threshold | Threshold in EUR | Annual candidate window in EUR | Flags whose value times 12 enters that window |
|:--|--:|--:|--:|:--|--:|
| Health-care allowance, 143 | 13,338 | 2,278 (17.08%) | 200 | 300–2,500 | 2,178 |
| Net AOW, 078 | 4,102 | 426 (10.39%) | 2,000 | 6,000–25,000 | 412 |
| Gross AOW, 076 | 15,782 | 985 (6.24%) | 2,000 | 6,000–30,000 | 911 |
| Child benefit, 140 | 6,199 | 223 (3.60%) | 300 | 500–12,000 | 217 |
| Net employer-1 wage, 012 | 17,195 | 976 (5.68%) | 1,500 | 5,000–150,000 | 798 |
| Gross employer-1 wage, 010 | 21,592 | 944 (4.37%) | 1,500 | 5,000–250,000 | 735 |
| Other net pension, 082 | 2,455 | 214 (8.72%) | 1,000 | 2,000–150,000 | 175 |

The first, third and fourth screens span all available releases where the
source fields retain these meanings; the older net AOW, wage and other
pension fields cover `ci08a`–`ci18k`. Pension branches also change: `ci13f082`
can include AOW plus other pensions, while `ci17j082` concerns other pensions.
Declared or label-identified
nonresponse and zero were excluded. The screens are not statutory payment
limits, full-year entitlement tests or questionnaire-invalid values.

The high candidate-window hit rates do not identify monthly entry. For
example, the allowance screen and its times-12 window mainly select
amounts between EUR 25 and 200 by construction. All 911 gross-AOW times-12
hits also fit times 13; all 217 child-benefit hits fit times 10 and 13,
and 197 fit times four. Many paired low wages already have ordinary net/gross
ratios: 697/833 comparable low-net-wage pairs need no rescaling to fit a
broad 0.5–1.1 ratio screen. Some low amounts have plausible neighbouring
annual values, but those observations do not distinguish multipliers or
exclude a genuine short receipt period.

**Detection and correction limits for periods.** First establish reference
year, receipt months, job/benefit start and end, gross/net definition and
any independently comparable annual total or bracket. Partial-year AOW,
short employment, refunds and small entitlements can be legitimate.
Flag unexplained period/scale patterns; treat multiplication as a candidate
only if independent evidence uniquely establishes the original period.
Neither a broad window nor repeated cross-wave values permits automatic
times-12/times-13 correction or invalid-to-missing treatment. Possible
understatement can materially affect benefit and wage analyses, but its
prevalence is not established by these screens.

#### Monetary tails and stronger component constraints

Other CI personal/component incomes and CD monetary amounts have extreme
tails, but rarity, legitimate high values, period differences and sparse
auxiliary evidence limit correction confidence. For example, the 2025
Housing screen finds five monthly-equivalent rents above EUR 5,000 among
982 eligible reports, and two purchase values above EUR 5 million among
2,162 after conversion only where the source explicitly identifies guilders.
These thresholds are review screens, not validity bounds. Across all 18 CD
waves, monthly-equivalent rent exceeds EUR 5,000 in 94/18,724 eligible
reports (0.50%), and converted purchase value exceeds EUR 5 million in
36/37,551 (0.10%). Included energy/service costs exceed the stated rent in
33/3,973 eligible positive pairs where the inclusion indicator is yes
(0.83%). That component/total conflict is a stronger flag than a high rent,
but it still does not identify the intended amount or reporting period.

Across CI, net annual wage exceeds 1.5 times the matching gross annual wage
in 344/18,083 paired employer/wage observations (1.90%). The wage fields
change with the employer-reporting scheme; for example, `ci25r372` is
annual gross wage and `ci25r439` its net counterpart. Annual taxable income
amounts are `337`/`338` rather than bracket field `226`. Annual gross wages
above EUR 1 million occur in 13/36,540 reports; annual taxable income above
EUR 1 million occurs in 32/36,526 after excluding the 2,680 CI23p
nonresponse codes from the earlier denominator. Reimbursements and differing gross/net
interpretations can complicate the paired screen, so none of these counts
is a demonstrated numerical error rate.

CI rent-arrears durations exceed 120 months in 60/302 eligible reports;
utilities-arrears durations do so in 85/291. The source permits 3–999
months, so these are suspicious but **not** violations of a twelve-month
maximum. In CD25r, only 3/249 complete eight-field mortgage sets differ from
their stated total by more than EUR 1. Requiring complete comparable
components and allowing rounding avoids a false claim of widespread
mortgage-accounting errors. There are 259/65,874 floor counts above ten.
The questionnaire asks about the respondent's own dwelling, so reporting
the whole apartment building is one possible explanation; a high count
alone does not prove this interpretation.

Across the 15 CW waves, none of 208,100 nonmissing weekly-hour field
observations exceeds 168 hours; 29 exceed a soft screen of 100 hours.
Hours above 100 are not proved wrong, and multiple job/activity fields
cannot be summed without checking overlap and reference periods.

**Detection and correction limits.** Preserve currency, period, gross/net,
personal/household, stock/flow and reference-year distinctions. Assets may
have genuine negative balances; income components may include losses;
deflation forecasts may be negative. Build flags from explicit units,
brackets and independently comparable components, not global sign rules
or a universal upper cap. A reported bracket constrains a range but does
not establish the exact amount or justify its midpoint as a repair. Do not
extend household-income donor or scale rules to other concepts by analogy.

**Priority rationale.** Monetary extremes can have large analytical effects,
but the assessed examples lack the prevalence-plus-identification advantage
of the higher-ranked candidates. A flag-only extension is useful; generic
rescaling, winsorisation or donor correction would carry substantial risk.

## Source recovery, negative findings and evidence limits

### An instrument omission requires release recovery, not respondent correction

`codebook_ci25r_EN_1.2.pdf` records that net-income questions `439`–`443`
were mistakenly omitted during June/July fieldwork and administered to
eligible respondents in September. The available `ci25r_EN_1.0p.sav`
contains only 16, 4, 46, 24 and 2 valid answers respectively in these
fields. These counts do not establish eligible-population missingness rates,
but they limit current-wave gross/net checks. The assessment cannot certify
that this SAV incorporates the later administration. Verify the corrected
release and follow-up provenance before interpreting those absences as
respondent nonresponse. A cleaner cannot reconstruct unasked income items
without fabricating information. This source-recovery prerequisite has
high practical importance but is outside automated value correction.

The occupation supplement `WorkSchoolingW10_isco08.sav` has 5,926 identifiers,
all matching `cw17j_EN_2.0p.sav` one-to-one. Its 3,452 observed codes include
195 labelled "not codable" values at `-9`; those are not 3,452 valid
occupation classifications. The current CW recipe does not integrate this
supplement into the later in-file occupation series. A verified supplement
join and compatible occupation taxonomy would improve completeness, but
this is a source-integration prerequisite, not evidence of respondent typos.

The CP substantive-scale screen found no values outside the allowed
domains after accounting for the known `999`/`-9` nonresponse regimes.
The extended screen covered 13,864,467 nonmissing labelled-scale cells;
LOT-R items contributed a separate 768,721 cells with no domain violations.
Its 4,971 corresponding raw sentinel cells are intentional nonresponse,
not 4,971 newly discovered errors; existing recipe handling covers those
regimes where supported. `cp26r` was available for raw-data screening beyond
the current recipe and local codebook coverage. That screening does not
certify a merge recipe or questionnaire specification for the new wave.

Two apparent additional domain problems were checked against the source
questionnaires. The continuous IOS sliders in `cp13f211`, `212`, `215`,
`216` use a coordinate range of **0–102**; all 184 observed values at
101/102 are permitted, not invalid percentages. In nine CH waves whose SAV
limitation labels omit code 5, there are 9,973 code-5 cells in 3,391 rows,
not fewer cells than rows. Of these, 8,556 cells in `ch11e`–`ch18k` have
explicit same-wave questionnaire support for 5 = "not at all". A blanket
1–4-domain rule would remove the most limited responses. The other 1,417
cells (483 rows) in `ch08b`/`ch10d` remain questionnaire/metadata
discrepancies requiring archive confirmation; flag their source contract,
preserve the responses and abstain from guessed recoding.
These controls demonstrate why raw maxima, missing labels or an assumed
standard scale cannot replace a release-specific source contract.

The CH none-plus-some health-condition screen found six contradictions;
one negative cigarette-count value in `ch15h130` violates the nonnegative
count domain. It warrants a narrow flag or explicit invalid-to-missing
treatment, not an absolute-value repair. Its isolated prevalence puts it
below the larger groups. These binary/count contradictions do not identify
an intended replacement response.
The CS organization screen found none. The CR screen did not identify a
comparable high-priority numerical cleaning group. These results justify
placing those checks below the diagnosed problems, not assuming that all
responses in those modules are valid. The CV bounded scale/category
interval screen covered 2,849 file-column instances and 15,362,235 eligible
cells; the 87 scale violations reported above were its only values beyond
those intervals. It did not test every possible categorical gap or every
cross-item semantic relation.

The assessment covers the stated local release set, not all files ever
published by the archive. It did not adjudicate respondents' intentions,
validate free text, benchmark future correction accuracy, or establish
which analytical models are sensitive to every flag. The CS mean comparison
is the one direct downstream sensitivity calculation reported here;
other impact statements identify mechanisms of possible distortion.

## Ordered to-do list derived from the assessment

Every future rule should declare its module, release and field scope,
required evidence, detection predicate, candidate constraints, confidence
and disposition. Preserve original values, flags and proposed values in
separate columns. Record respondent/wave/month and field identity, input
file hashes, rule and recipe versions, observed value, evidence, competing
candidates, final disposition and reason in the audit ledger. A flag-only
run must be possible. Rules must abstain when prerequisites are absent,
and review disagreements must remain visible. No item below authorizes
implementation or changes to the source datasets.

Before these rule-development priorities, verify the CI25r follow-up
release when those omitted income fields are needed. Source recovery is a
prerequisite for that analysis, not a numerical replacement rule. Likewise,
supplement integration must verify identifiers, taxonomy and nonresponse
meaning before expanding occupation coverage.

1. **Normalize source-specific nonresponse before numerical cleaning.**
   First place reflects the 52.68% household-income code exposure in CI23p,
   the tested cleaner proposal path, and the 48.71% CA20g respondent exposure.
   Develop exact release/field code detection for all three CI23p amounts,
   both CA20g code families and source-confirmed CH unknown amounts and
   categories. Put
   nonresponse classification before sign/scale/donor rules, and retain
   typed missingness or an explicit unknown category rather than fabricate
   an amount or erase a meaningful nonresponse category. Safeguards must test
   exact target binding, raw and merged metadata, positive and negative
   legitimate controls, routing, and uncertain DK/refusal subtypes. The
   diagnostic runner must preserve original values and a per-cell ledger.
   Expected improvement: prevent missing codes from driving wealth/income
   estimates or entering inappropriate correction proposals.
2. **Preserve category meanings across instrument versions and exports.**
   Second place reflects broad exposure and several source-identified,
   conservative normalization opportunities. Develop release-specific
   holiday crosswalks, a separate CS12e loneliness representation with a
   format flag, category-plus-score representations for CF outsourcing,
   and correct CI15h label metadata without shifting its values. Obtain
   authoritative CV mapping before applying any minus-one repair, and
   define an explicit coarser taxonomy for CW education attended (`s008`,
   recipe alias `q008`) only where defensible.
   Safeguards must preserve source labels/declarations, missing reasons,
   top-coding, score applicability and unmapped distinctions; test that the
   export/reimport sweep cannot erase newly derived substantive categories.
   Expected improvement: prevent artificial longitudinal shifts and loss
   of real outcomes without asserting unsupported measurement equivalence.
3. **Validate CH and CS time inputs under their separate source contracts.**
   Third place combines a larger CH impossible-hours group with measured
   CS mean distortion and strong unit/bound constraints. Inventory every
   relevant hour/minute pair by wave; validate single-activity daily/weekly
   budgets and only source-specified residual bounds. Invalidate a dependent
   CS total when its input is invalid. For CH exact-multiple patterns, retain
   competing additive/alternative-unit interpretations unless independent
   evidence resolves them. Safeguards must distinguish empty from zero,
   overlapping activities, deleted fields and score normalization from
   source-value correction. Expected improvement: protect activity scores
   and time-use estimates from impossible inputs without assuming a unit
   repair or halving legitimate durations.
4. **Add probability-set and ordered-interval validation.** This ranks
   fourth because almost one third of the CI25r grids are incoherent under
   necessary constraints, with corroborating smaller problems in CI/CH.
   Use wave-specific displayed thresholds, bounds, nested-event order,
   disjoint sums and endpoint order. The constrained-correction policy
   should abstain from numerical replacement; offer flag/review and explicit
   missing-set dispositions. Preserve tolerance choices and overlapping
   reasons, and require sensitivity comparisons for exclusion. Expected
   improvement: prevent incoherent sets from silently determining estimated
   expectations and uncertainty without manufacturing respondents' beliefs.
5. **Develop conservative anthropometry checks.** Fifth place reflects
   amplified effects on BMI, but softer identification than the time-domain
   failures above. Combine units,
   instrument bounds, broad plausibility, derived BMI and temporal evidence.
   Permit a correction candidate only when independent observations support
   a unique unit/decimal repair; otherwise flag or use an explicit
   invalid-to-missing policy. Safeguards must accommodate genuine extremes
   and health changes, avoid smoothing, and ledger all rejected candidates.
   Expected improvement: reduce leverage from scale errors while preserving
   clinically unusual observations.
6. **Add clinical-use, life-event and duration consistency rules for CH, CW and CF.**
   These come sixth because contradictions are defensible but usually sparse
   and do not identify the erroneous field. Compare binary service-use
   answers with counts only for the same service and reference period.
   Include narrow nonnegative-count checks for the isolated tobacco anomaly.
   Decode year categories, use
   conservative birth-year intervals, distinguish relationship types and
   actual/planned events, and check duration against age. Allow constrained
   auxiliary recovery only from validated dates or correctly indexed
   rosters; otherwise abstain and flag. Expected improvement: protect event
   ordering and duration analyses without inventing onset years or family
   histories.
7. **Add monthly demographic and roster review checks.** Seventh position
   reflects widespread analytical use, a larger partner-recording boundary,
   and uncertain source precedence. Check identity/provenance,
   birthday-tolerant age progression, demographic discontinuities and
   same-month household constraints. Flag the 2014–2017 partner/position
   disagreement without choosing a source automatically.
   Safeguards must honor 9+ top-coding, incomplete rosters and legitimate
   administrative corrections; prohibit nearest-month substitution and
   majority-value overwrites or assumptions that nonparticipation means
   departure. Expected improvement: expose covariate and
   equivalisation risks while retaining valid household transitions.
8. **Develop evidence-based period checks and other financial/housing/workload
   review flags.** This comes last because even frequent small annual amounts
   do not identify a reporting error, and extremes often remain legitimate.
   Use reference-year receipt/eligibility, recorded currency/period,
   comparable gross/net pairs and bracket/component constraints. Require
   independent evidence for a unique period or scale correction; otherwise
   retain a flag and competing candidates. Safeguards must preserve signed
   balances, losses, partial-year receipt and legitimate tiny amounts;
   a times-12 plausibility window is not a correction rule. Do not transfer
   household-income caps, donor rules or generic clipping. Expected
   improvement: make analytical sensitivity and review needs visible while
   minimizing false corrections of unusual but real observations.
